title: [PDF] Stallinga-Ganzevoort Holland-Canada Emigration Collection, 1890 ...
content: The collection consists of correspondence, reports, lists, and pamphlets regarding emigration (mostly in English), including correspondence from and about individual immigrants (mostly in Dutch). Reel 1: Folder nr.13 (former Rijksarchief at The Hague, nowadays National Archive): corre-spondence Centrale Stichting Landbouw Emigratie, 1938-December 1948: letters of the Stichting Landverhuizing Nederland (SLN) concerning recommendations, procedures, tests and withdrawals of individual emigrants, files are mostly on Canada and consist of correspondence with the Christelijke Emigratie Centrale. Folder nr.118: Jan.-May 1948: files and reports of emigrants in Canada (personal informa- tion of individual immigrants), some letters of A.S. Tuinman en J. Reel 4: Folder nr.119: Correspondence A.S. Tuinman with Dep.of Mines and Resources, accounts of Dutch emigrants to Canada (Jan.-Dec.1948), emigration procedures (June 1948). Folder nr.122: Nov.1948-June 1949: emigration procedures, annual report of A.S. Tuinman’s activities in 1948, letters about the Immigration Committee of the Christian Reformed Church, emigrant transport by KLM, letters of the Canadian Department of Mines and Resources, complaints about emigrants, numerous personal files of emigrants.

title: Dutch immigrants | Social Sciences and Humanities | Research Starters | EBSCO Research
content: The first wave began in the early 17th century, fueled by the Dutch West Indies Company's efforts to explore and colonize new territories, leading to the establishment of Fort Nassau, one of the earliest European settlements in North America. The second wave, during the mid-19th century, was primarily driven by religious tensions within the Netherlands, prompting many Dutch Reformed Church members to seek refuge and establish communities in the American Midwest. Throughout these periods, Dutch immigrants brought their cultural and religious traditions with them, leading to the formation of distinct Dutch-American communities that preserved aspects of their heritage. Despite a general trend of assimilation into mainstream American culture, many descendants maintain connections to their Dutch roots, exemplified by the celebration of tulip festivals in various U.S. cities and the ongoing presence of Dutch churches. In Canada, Dutch immigration was closely linked to U.S. trends, particularly post-World War II, as many Dutch families sought opportunities in a country offering land and employment.
